**Author rebuttal:**

Main difficulties compared to generic object detection: we already provide the details of the difference between YDLD and other detection datasets. Specifically, we mentioned the relation between our YDLD and tiny object detection (TOD) with statistics in MC-Sec. 3.4 (Data statistics). In addition, we explained the difference between YDLD and MS-COCO, which are considered as a generic object detection set, in SP-Sec A. More details of the YDLD Dataset of the supplementary (SP) material. These are the main intrinsic challenges of our YDLD: (1) much tinier objects than generic OD datasets. Figure 3 of the SP material supports it well. 68% of the light source objects in our YDLD fall within the very tiny ($[0^2, 8^2)$) and the tiny ($[8^2, 16^2)$) size categories, whereas only 12% of the objects in the MS-COCO dataset belong to these size ranges (2) YDLD have fewer distinctive visual features compared to typical detection objects. This is due to the similar appearance between light sources as shown in SP-Fig. 1. Therefore, the overall mAP score is much lower about two times (e.g., DINO mAP: 25.6% (YDLD), 50.1% (COCO)). However, we admit that the more details of our dataset challenges should be explained better in our paper. Therefore, we will revise our paper with this discussion.



 

The future direction of YDLD: light detection can be a fundamental and core technology in handling other downstream tasks. Most of all, LD is beneficial for understanding the behaviors of vehicles in night driving. Therefore, we will plan to launch a vehicle path and action recognition benchmark challenge based on vehicle action recognition methods [1, 2, 3]. To this end, we will expand the class taxonomy of the YDLD dataset (e.g., vehicle headlights, taillights, turn signals, etc). In addition, LD is also very essential for glare or artifact removals [4, 5, 6] since discrimination between the light source and other sources is needed. Therefore, the extended benchmark of light detection and glare removal is planned in our next research. Also, as recommenced by R3, de-blurring for low light images [7] can be another crucial extension using YDLD since inter camera motion between consecutive frames can be predicted by detecting light sources [8, 9].

**Lack of Limitation**

> [R1C2]. The paper's focus on nighttime and evening driving scenarios may limit its applicability.
>
> [R1C7]. No. I cannot find a sufficient description of the limitations of this paper in section 6.
>
> [R2C1]. Limitations are mostly not discussed. The future work section mentions what the authors plan to add in the future (sunlight class, pixel-wise labeling), but there is no real discussion about the limitations, if any, of this proposed dataset.
>
> [R3C9]. There are too few types of light sources.

We agreed that there is a need to discuss the limitations of this study in more detail to further improve this research. Accordingly, we would like to elaborate on the specific limitations of LD methodology and our YDLD dataset.

 

**The limitation of light source detection**

 

**Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) for TOD:** Albeit we present a lightness focal (LF) loss to suppress false positives (FP) and lightness attention prior, some FPs are not removed well. To understand this in depth, we visualized failure cases of FP reduction in Fig. 2. We observed that IoU scores of boxes are very low although they are located nearby at the box with a maximum classification score. For a more detailed analysis, we make the following additional evaluation in this rebuttal. We present the variations of IoU scores for two canonical box sizes 19 × 15 and 104 ×107, which are the averaged bounding box sizes of YDLD and MS-COCO, as shown in SP-Table 2. To this end, we replicate each box, shift the generated box toward vertical and horizontal directions by one pixel per iteration, and measure IoU scores between the original reference and shifted boxes. In Fig. 1-(a), IoU scores of the small-sized boxes more steeply decrease than those of the large-sized boxes. Also, the low IoU scores are because the current IoU matching algorithm [1] used in this work basically evaluates the scores with the ratio of an overlapping area over a union area between boxes. As a result, even a slight box mismatch can lead to the degradation of an IoU significantly.

Based on this insight, we conduct an experiment to investigate the distributions of IoU scores on our YDLD and MS-COCO for applying a detector. To this end, we randomly select 1,500 images from each dataset and perform inference using original PAA [2] with a confidence score threshold of 0.1. Subsequently, we select boxes which are best matched with GT and measure IoU scores between overlapped boxes with the selected boxes. Figure 1-(b) shows the comparison of histograms and the number of unfiltered and overlapped boxes by the NMS algorithm with different IoU thresholds (colored curve in each sub-figure). To reduce redundancy, the NMS eliminates overlapped boxes which have the IoU score greater than or equal to the IoU threshold given a box. For example, all overlapped boxes are eliminated when the IoU threshold is 0, and most boxes remain when the IoU threshold is 1.0 except for a reference box with the highest confidence. For MS-COCO, the yellowed curve for the IoU threshold range of $[0.3, 0.8]$ is almost flat. This result shows that the NMS is lower sensitive to the IoU threshold and robustly works well on MS-COCO. In contrast, the gradient for YDLD is consistently steep, and it is hard to select the optimal or generalized IoU threshold since a threshold largely affects precision and recall rates. Therefore, we encounter the trade-off issue of false positive and false negatives when tunning the NMS IoU threshold. From this analysis, we recognize the necessity of NMS for TOD. As a hint of this, we see that the probabilistic box alignment of the RFLA method [3] can be leveraged for the NMS.

**Multi-Modal Light Detection:** Including our YDLD dataset, most light detection datasets consist of RGB images. However, even recent detector tends to produce false positives due to light scattering and interception effects such as glare as shown in Fig. 2. To solve this problem, we expect multi-modal light detection using RGB-T (thermal images) can be one of the solutions. To verify the possibility of this, we conduct light detection using PAA [2] on the KAIST multispectral pedestrian detection dataset [4] consisting of RGB+T images. As shown in Fig. 3, the RGB image shows false positives of carlight (blue bounding box) in the area with reflected light (magenta box). On the other hand, in thermal images, the temperature of the reflected light is low and the reflection is not detected, so no false positives occur. Otherwise, carlights are detected accurately in the light source area. As a result, we expect that RGB-T image can be an effective way to achieve more robust light detection in real driving scenes.

**The limitation of YDLD datsaset** 

**Absence of a sunlight source class:** As mentioned in the paper's conclusion, YDLD does not include a sunlight class. There are two important reasons: (1) as shown in MC-Table3, most existing light detection studies already focused on detecting sun light areas. In addition, we received stronger requests to build YDLD due to the absence of multi-light sources for night driving from industrial or education institutes. (2) difficult and costly annotation to cover multi-source detection: it is not tricky to limit a binary sunlight detection problem or annotate vague regions of a sun source. However, it is necessary for accurate region annotation for multi-class detections and the precise annotation of sunlight source requires costly pix-wise labeling. But, it would be beyond the detection task we handled. Therefore, we will plan to contain this sunlight class and expand our work to the instance segmentation task during day/evening/night time shortly.

**Taxonomy expansion**: YDLD does not consider indoor lights or signboards as foreground until now since they are less significant for the other three classes under night driving. However, to improve the generality of YDLD, we will treat the neon signs, signboards, indoor lighting, and decorative lights as distinct light-source classes. In addition, as mentioned MC-Sec. 3.1, light source detection is very effective in understanding other object contexts. Therefore, it is very worth including object annotations related to lights such as a vehicle or pole to extend this work to other tasks.

We agree with the suggestion that the related works section in our paper should be strengthened. To address this, we have expanded the appendix to include a more comprehensive review of studies and datasets related to glare and light, tiny object detection datasets, and object detection and SSOD (Semi-Supervised Object Detection). The details of the added related works can be found as follows.

 

**Applications related with light source:** Light detection is a fundamental research area in various computer vision tasks. It is important to remove glare and flare caused by light sources, as they can degrade image quality. Since light sources, glare, and flare are highly correlated, datasets have been proposed to learn this prior relationship. [1] creates and releases a semi-synthetic dataset by simulating the physical phenomena related to flare and synthesizing flare and glare onto clean images. Flare7K [2] focuses on glare and lens flare removal in low-light conditions, especially at night. Similar to [1], it uses synthetic flare and glare. Additionally, the more image enhancement research has been conducted in low-light conditions by utilizing light sources. [3] proposes a network that predicts the inverse camera response function to improve the visibility of low-light images while removing noise and glare. [4] proposes an unsupervised approach that combines a layer decomposition network with a light-effects suppression network.

 

On the other hand, in road driving environments, important signals for making decisions are primarily conveyed through light sources (e.g., traffic lights, brake lamps, and turn signals). Consequently, research has been conducted to recognize and detect these critical light sources. [5] proposes the rear-lamp recognition in low-light images method using color cross-correlation symmetry analysis to detect and track vehicles by identifying their taillights. [6] studies for recognizing vehicle headlights by learning a vehicle mask. Additionally, the LISA Traffic Light Dataset [7] is built to detect traffic light and learn the signal.

 

**Tiny object detection:** Tiny objects refer to objects smaller than 32×32 pixels, based on the MS-COCO standard. Due to their small size, tiny object detection (TOD) is still considered as a challenging task. To address the TOD problem, various datasets and methods have been proposed.

 

DOTA [8] (Dataset for Object Detection in Aerial Images) dataset handles the aerial image domain and includes 15 classes such as vehicles, airplanes, and roundabouts. AI-TOD (Tiny Object Detection in Aerial Images) [9] dataset also focuses on the aerial image domain and covers 8 classes, including airplanes, bridges, and swimming pools. TinyPerson [10] dataset is based on images with a long distance with massive background and aims to distinguish between people and the background. Visdrone [11] dataset is based on drone images of urban environments and includes classes such as people, cars, and trucks. 


To address the TOD problem, tiny object oriented methods are proposed. FSANet [12] extracts more discriminative features for tiny objects by utilizing feature-and-spatial alignment and incremental optimization techniques. RFLA [13] improves the performance of tiny object detection by proposing a Gaussian receptive-based label assignment method.

**Object Detection:** Object detection (OD) is a fundamental task in computer vision. It involves simultaneously classifying and locating objects in images.

 

Initially, R-CNN [14] is proposed to solve object detection using convolutional neural networks. However, R-CNN has the speed issue since it extracts each object region features via iterative feature propagation. To address it, Fast R-CNN [15] is introduced to extract regions of interest (RoI) features efficiently from a shared convolution map. Faster R-CNN [16] proposes a Region Proposal Network (RPN). This allows the network to learn the region proposal process internally, improving speed. Later, Mask R-CNN [17] introduces RoIAlign for more precise object detection at the pixel level.

 

These two-stage object detectors offer high detection accuracy but are slow. To overcome this, single-stage object detectors are proposed. Unlike two-stage detectors, they perform object classification and localization in a single step. YOLO (You Only Look Once) [18] enables real-time object detection by processing the entire image with a single network. RetinaNet [19] addresses the class imbalance problem by introducing the focal loss, which is applied to one-stage detectors. Additionally, research has been conducted on label assignment techniques to effectively match anchors with ground truth to improve object detector accuracy [13, 20]. PAA [20] adaptively divides anchors into positive and negative samples by fitting a probability distribution to the anchor scores.

 

Recently, there have been efforts to apply the transformer to object detection. The transformer is specialized in extracting global context, allowing them to more effectively understand relationships between objects and capture global information. DETR [21], Deformable DETR [22], and DINO [23] are representative of the transformer-based object detection models. Deformable DETR [22] enhances the multi-head attention complexity in object detection by learning sampling points on key feature maps. DINO [23] improves the convergence speed of DETR by using positive and negative noise queries.

 

**Semi-supervision for object detection:** We discuss some SSOD methods in brief. Refer to [24] for more details of SSOD. The common way is to generate pseudo annotations from a trained detector (i.e., teacher) on unlabeled or augmented samples, and then exploit them for training a target detector (i.e., student). Exponential moving average [25] is used for updating a teacher. SoftTeacher [24] improves pseudo-label quality gradually. ConstistentTeacher [26] presents an anchor assignment for pseudo boxes. MixTeacher [27] performs multi-scale pseudo-labeling using FPN. Inspired by these works, we incorporate our lightness focal loss into the detection-based MeanTeacher [26] to improve generalization and discrimination abilities.

**Handling Complex Lighting Conditions in YDLD Dataset Annotations**

>[R3C3]. In real-world scenarios, the lighting environment is generally very complex, especially in today of high light pollution. There are often multiple interfering stray light, multi-light merging, false light sources, and area overexposure in the image. How does the light annotation of the LD dataset handle these situations? Please give a detailed description.

As you pointed out, it can indeed be challenging to distinguish individual light sources when multiple sources merge into one, or when the image quality is degraded due to overexposure or low illumination. However, this study is in the early stages of multi-source light detection, making it difficult to address all these complex situations. Therefore, we performed the annotations by excluding the unusual or complex cases you mentioned.

 

Therefore, overexposed images were excluded. In situations like multi-light merging, annotations were made as tightly as possible around the light sources, excluding glare areas, when the sources can be distinguished as mentioned in MC-Sec. 3.2. However, in cases where the light sources were too densely gathered or too small to clearly distinguish their boundaries, no annotations were made to avoid the model learning incorrect light source knowledge. Nonetheless, to enhance the generality of the light detector, such ambiguous situations must also be considered. Therefore, these situations will be addressed in future research to enable light source detection in a wider range of scenarios.

**Detailed Description of the Proposed SS-FLD**



>[R3C4]. Authors may need to come up with a complete model framework of their own LD methods, so that we can clearly understand the role of Lightness Focal Loss and Lightness Spatial Attention Prior.
>
>[R3C5].What are the parts of the complete loss function of the LD method in this article?
>
>[R3C6]. It's a pity that I didn't understand how exactly Lightnes Spattyar Atentin Priol did it.
>
>[R3C7]. The two parts（4.1 Lightness Focal Loss and 4.2 Lightness Spatial Attention Prior） seem to be a bit of a mess.
>
>[R3C8].The definition of SS-FL is also confusing. The SS-FL I understand is a total detection loss of SS-FLD in equation（3）.If yes, what is the core focus of the SS-FLD section? Only another loss function? Please give more details



**[R3C4]:** Thank you for your valuable suggestions to further improve our paper. Even though we provide the overall framework in MC-Fig. 3, it is a generalized SSOD-based framework to include any recent detector. Thus, we agreed that details of the used detector are beneficial to understanding the connection points between our SS-FLD method and the used detector deeply. However, it is not easy to contain the structure of a detector due to the page limit, we will provide a complete detection framework including RFLD and DINO with our SS-FLD in the supplementary material.

 

**[R3C5]:** To further explain our SS-FLD total detection loss defined in MC-Eq. (3), we first describe each total loss used in DINO and RFLA. Here, we omit the index $l$ (c.f. $u$) denoting labeled data for simplicity unless other mentioned.

The loss of DINO $L_{DINO}$ is defined as $L_{DINO}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[\lambda_{cls} \cdot L_{cls}(f(\mathbf{x}\_i), \mathbf{y}\_i) + \lambda_{L1} \cdot L_{L1} (f(\mathbf{x}\_i), \mathbf{y}\_i) + \lambda_{GIoU} \cdot L_{GIoU}(f(\mathbf{x}\_i), \mathbf{y}\_i)]$

$\mathbf{x}\_i$ and $\mathbf{y}\_i$ are the input image and class label of $i$-th sample. $f(\cdot)$ is the object detector network. $\lambda_{cls}$, $\lambda_{L1}$, and $\lambda_{GIoU}$ are the coefficient of each loss. $L_{DINO}$ exploits the focal loss [1]  as the classification loss $L_{cls}$. L1 loss $L_{L1}$ and GIoU (generalized Intersection over Union loss) loss [2] $L_{GIoU}$ are used for the regression losses. 

The detection loss of RFLA is defined as $L_{RFLA} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}[L_{cls}(f(\mathbf{x}\_i), \mathbf{y}\_i) + L_{DIoU}(f(\mathbf{x}\_i), \mathbf{y}\_i)]$. It uses the focal loss and DIoU (Distance Intersection over Union) loss [3] $L_{DIoU}$ for classification and regression, respectively. 

To apply SS-FLD for each detector, we replace $L_{cls}$ with the lightness focal loss defined in MC-Eq. (2). In addition, we utilize these losses on labeled and unlabeled data to perform semi-supervised learning suited for light detection. The complete loss function of semi-supervision is in MC-Eq. (3). $L_{reg}$ loss for the DINO and RFLA can be replaced with $L_{L1} + L_{GIoU}$ and $L_{DIoU}$. We are sorry again for less details of this explanation and will include these complete losses in our supplementary material.

**[R3C6]:** We are sorry for some unclear explanation of our spatial attention prior. Although we made the detailed explanation of the generation process and geometrical meaning of the prior map $\phi(\mathbf{d}\_c) $in MC-Sec. 4.1 and 4.2, we realized that the effect of the prior is not clear rather in the LF loss Eq. (2). In addition, the explanation of predicting $\phi(\mathbf{d}\_c) = \frac{1}{w \times h} \sum_{i=cx-0.5w}^{cx+0.5w} \sum_{j=cy-0.5h}^{cy+0.5h} \Phi(i,j,c)$ with the learned prior map $\Phi(i,j,c)$ and detection box $(\mathbf{d}\_c)$ is better to relocate it below Eq. (2) for easy understanding since $\Phi(i,j,c)$ is input of Eq. (2).

The output of $\phi(\mathbf{d}_c)$ is the averaged occurrence score within a box region $\mathbf{d}_c$ when placing $\mathbf{d}_c$ onto the learned prior map $\Phi(i,j,c)$ as the above equation. This can determine how much the predicted box is reliable in consideration of geometrical dependency between a light class and a road scene. If $\mathbf{d}_c$ is predicted in a higher occurrence region of $\Phi(i,j,c)$ (red areas in the Lightness prior map in MC-Fig. 5), $\phi(\mathbf{d}_c)$ is getting increased, but the LF loss becomes decreased in return. Otherwise, the LF loss is getting increased as $\phi(\mathbf{d}_c)$ decreases. This is particularly useful for preventing to over-increase the LF loss from indistinguishable detections predicted within high-occurrence regions and penalizing inaccurate detection within low-occurrence regions. We have proved the effect of this from the ablation study in MC-Table 8. By comparing (M1) and (M3), our spatial prior achieves the mAP gain by 2.9%.

**[R3C7]:** We agree with your constructive comment. We will re-write and re-organize sections 4.1 and 4.2 as follows: we will revise section 4.1, "Lightness Focal Loss." It now includes only the explanation of the lightness focal Loss and each term of the LF loss. Then, we will move the details of generating the lightness prior map (in lines L.198–L.207, page 6) to Section 4.2, "Lightness Spatial Attention Prior". Also, we include the effects of the attention prior map discussed above [R3C6] in Sec. 4.2. We expect that this change improves the readability of each section much more.

**The reason of Trafficsignallights achieve higher mAP than Streetlights and Carlights** 

>[R1C3]. Detecting streetlights and car lights appears to be more challenging than detecting traffic signal lights (Table 4 in the Supplementary Material). What are the possible reasons? Is it because the traffic signal lights have color?



Due to the importance of traffic lights for road environment, it is usually installed in locations where they are not occluded or contaminated by other objects or light sources. Also, as mentioned by R1, a similar or distinctive light color could affect this. On the other hand, car lights are usually occluded more frequently by other objects and they have a similar color.

 

In addition, we expect that the lightness attention prior also contributed to improving traffic light detection. Due to the more restricted locations of the traffic lights, the distribution of attention prior is narrowed more than the distribution of the car lights as shown in MC-Fig. 5. Thus, the FPs out of the distribution are suppressed more easily. In Table 2, we make the additional comparison between the original focal loss and our LF loss with spatial attention prior. This is the detailed analysis between (M1) and (M3) for each class in MC-Table. 8. Our lightness spatial attention prior increases 3.2 points for TrafficSignallight by leveraging the scene context. On the other hand, detecting car lights is the most challenging problem since it shows the lowest mAP scores as shown in SP-Table 4. Despite this difficulty, we achieve the impressive improvement of 3.2 points for the Carlight. This implies that the light occurrence probability is co-related to the scene geometrical context. As a result, our spatial attention prior increases mAP by about 2.9 points. These results show that our prior is well-learned for the geometrical context and is beneficial to improving the discriminability between light classes.

**Analysis of failure cases through confusion matrix and qualitative results** 

>[R1C5]. The experimental results shown are not objective. Although the overall results are low, the visualization results presented in the paper are acceptable. Statistics on negative results and failure cases should be provided (Figure 3 in the Supplementary Material displays performance results for different sizes of bounding boxes, but lacks accompanying discussions).
>
>[R1C6]. The degree of confusion between different classes of light detection should be presented. The ratio of false negative and false positive should also be provided. This information is very useful for understanding this task.



We agreed with the suggestion that failure cases are necessary to enhance the objectivity of our experiments. While we did present failure cases in SP-Fig. 2, these were primarily failures related to surrounding objects or cases where the detection did not align with the global geometrical context. To show more failure cases, we have added the results in Fig. 2. False negatives usually happen for very tiny and twisted lights. To remedy this, increase the generality of our YDLD to contain these hard samples. On the other hand, false positives often occur in areas with strong glare or when the light source is tiny. These are closely related to the NMS issue of tiny objects as already discussed in common issue 2 in this rebuttal.

 

To understand false positive and negative cases in depth, we have presented a confusion matrix in Fig. 4 as recommended by R1. To show the effects of our method, we make the comparison of confusion matrices for DINO and DINO w/t SS-FLD. In this evaluation, we consider a true positive when the predicted and a GT box has more than a certain IoU score. Following the standard mAP evaluation on MS-COCO, we change the IoU threshold at [0.5 (start):0.95(end):0.05(step)] and evaluate a confusion matrix per IoU threshold. We then present the confusion matrices in terms of precision and recall rates in Fig. 4-(a) and (b). 

 

For DINO, the average false discovery rate (FDR; $\frac{FP}{TP+TP}$) and false negative rate (FNR; $\frac{FN}{TP + FN}$) are 69.39% and 72.50%, respectively. On the other hand, for DINO with SS-FLD, the FDR and FNR are 62.72% and 69.69%. Thus, our SS-FLD reduces the rates by 3.67% and 2.81%. Remarkably, our method improves these rates for all the classes. We assert that these gains originated from our LF loss and semi-supervision. Interestingly, both detectors showed few false detections between light source classes and more confusion for the discrimination between light source and background. It might be due to light reflection, scattering, complex scene clutters, tiny light sizes, etc. Therefore, it is also related to the limitations of our YDLD and current detectors as mentioned in common issue 2.

title.value: Comments on the paper titled 'A New Multi-Source Light Detection Benchmark and Semi-Supervised Focal Light Detection'

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper presents the YouTube Driving Light Detection (YDLD) dataset, which is used to detect lights from multiple sources in driving scenarios. Additionally, a new lightness focal loss is introduced to enhance detection accuracy by penalizing misclassified samples and incorporating a spatial attention prior. Furthermore, a semi-supervised focal light detection (SS-FLD) method is developed to improve performance by utilizing both labeled and unlabeled data. The evaluations demonstrate that their approach improves mAP scores across different detectors.

review.value:
+ **Quality**:

    **pros**
   + The paper is well-structured and provides a detailed explanation of the methods proposed, along with their motivations.
   + The new dataset YDLD may stimulate further research that could be beneficial for autonomous driving.
    
    **cons**
    + The paper provides a detailed introduction to comparing datasets and conducting benchmark experiments. However, the analysis and explanations regarding the challenges of the LD task and its specialization compared to generic detection are limited. 
    
+ **Clarity**:
   + The writing is clear, and it effectively utilizes figures and tables to illustrate the key points of the datasets as well as the performance of the designed loss and framework.

+ **Originality and significance**:

  + The proposed YDLD dataset is a new multi-source light detection dataset that has received less exploration compared to other object detection tasks.
  + The paper's focus on nighttime and evening driving scenarios may limit its applicability.

strengths.value:
+ The dataset can fill the existing gap in benchmarks for object detection, which includes annotations for various types of traffic-related lighting and is sourced from different countries.
+ The proposed lightness focal loss and SS-FLD method have been shown to be effective in detecting light.
+ The paper is written clearly and has a well-structured format.
+ The data and code will be publicly available.

title.value: Useful dataset for multi-source light detection

summary_and_contributions.value: This contribution presents a new annotated dataset for multi-source light detection. Specifically, 3 classes of light sources are annotated for street images collected during the dark hours of the day. In addition to this, a new lightness focal loss which penalizes miss-classified samples more and a lightness spatial attention prior by reflecting a global scene context are presented that significantly improve light source detection. Comparison with many existing methods is also included. Overall, this is a well-constructed dataset for this specific task.

review.value:
Quality: the dataset appears to be well-constructed, with a significant human labeling effort to both label the light sources and to ensure the quality of labeling. The dataset is diverse and comprehensive. 

Clarity: the description is well-written and generally is relatively easy to follow.  The steps taken to construct the dataset are well described. There is also a detailed description of how the newly proposed lightness focal loss is derived and lightness spatial attention prior is introduced. These descriptions perhaps are not as straightforward to understand, but they should be comprehendible by those working in this field.

Originality: there are existing datasets, however the proposed dataset here goes beyond the state of the art by the size, classes, and labeling quality.

strengths.value:
The main strength of this dataset is in the quality of labels, including very small light sources. These are difficult to label and therefore frequently are omitted in other datasets. Also, the discrimination among 3 classes makes of light sources makes this dataset to stand out. 

Newly proposed lightness focal loss is also an interesting addition to the field.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: The authors already pointed out one possible direction for improvements: adding examples with the sun as one of the light sources. This will greatly extend the applicability of the dataset.

limitations.value: Limitations are mostly not discussed. The future work section mentions what the authors plan to add in the future (sunlight class, pixel-wise labeling), but there is no real discussion about the limitations, if any, of this proposed dataset.

correctness.value: The dataset seems to be constructed in a sound way. Multiple people labeled each frame and a quality control was put in place. The proposed lightness focal loss and a lightness spatial attention prior seem to make sense.

clarity.value:
The paper is generally well-written, except for the typos and occasional grammar errors. There are many typos, here are a few examples:

public available -> publicly available
In specific, -> specifically
convey the different -> convey different
is a still -> is still a
More specially -> Specifically

Abstract needs improvements. 

Many terms are not defined, e.g., what is mAP?

relation_to_prior_work.value: Relevant datasets and methods are discussed in details and are used in relevant comparisons.

documentation.value: A github with the relevant documentation and code is provided. However, only a small subset of the dataset is available for download via a link to "A hundred sample images of the YDLD dataset".

1.In the introduction section, the background and difficulties of LD task are not adequately described.

title.value: A New Multi-Source Light Detection Benchmark and Semi-Supervised Focal Light Detection

abstract.value:
This paper addresses a multi-source light detection (LD) problem from vehicles, traffic signals, and streetlights under driving scenarios. Albeit it is crucial for autonomous driving and night vision, this problem has not been yet focused on as much as other object detection (OD). One of the main reasons is the absence of a public available LD benchmark dataset. Therefore, we construct a new large LD dataset consisting of different light sources via heavy annotation: YouTube Driving Light Detection dataset (YDLD). Compared to the existing LD datasets, our dataset has much more images and box annotations for multi-source lights. We also provide rigorous statistical analysis and transfer learning comparison of other well-known detection benchmark datasets to prove the generality of our YDLD.

For the recent object detectors, we achieve the extensive comparison results on YDLD. However, they tend to yield the low mAP scores due to the intrinsic challenges of LD caused by very tiny size and similar appearance. To resolve those, we design a novel lightness focal loss which penalizes miss-classified samples more and a lightness spatial attention prior by reflecting a global scene context. In addition, we develop a semi-supervised focal light detection (SS-FLD) by embedding our lightness focal loss into the semi-supervised object detection (SSOD). We prove that our methods can consistently boost mAP to the variety of types of recent detectors on YDLD. We will open both YDLD and SS-FLD code at https://github.com/YDLD-dataset/YDLD.

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

            updated_note.content = {

                        venue_fullname=venue_name,

                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
